frase_gancho.texto: The mother goddess who gives life and claims it back, made of serpents.

puente_narrativo.texto: From the mother we move on to the daughter who rose up against her. Step up to a stone head with closed eyes and cheeks adorned with bells: Coyolxauhqui.

guion_corto.texto: You are standing before Coatlicue, “she of the skirt of serpents,” one of the most impressive sculptures of the ancient world. She stands more than two and a half meters tall and has no human head: in its place, two serpents face each other in profile and form a monstrous face. Around her neck she wears a necklace of severed hands and hearts, with a skull hanging at the center; her skirt is a braid of rattlesnakes, and her feet end in eagle claws. She is the mother of Huitzilopochtli, the god of the Sun and of war, and she embodies the Earth: the one who gives the maize and the one who receives the dead. She was found in 1790, beneath the Main Square.

guion_largo.texto:
To understand Coatlicue, you have to climb, in your imagination, the hill of Coatepec, the “hill of the serpent.” There the goddess was sweeping, the myth says, when a little ball of feathers fell from the sky. She tucked it into her chest and became pregnant. Her children, the moon [Coyolxauhqui](mna_s06_coyolxauhqui) and the four hundred star siblings, the Centzonhuitznahua, felt dishonored and decided to kill her. At that critical moment the story pauses. What happened next you will learn at the following piece.

Now look at her face, or rather, her lack of one. From the severed neck spring two streams of blood that are two serpents, and as they look at each other in profile they form, between them, eyes, fangs, and forked tongues. The sculptor did not want to show a woman, but an idea: life that springs from a body that gives itself up. It is an image that frightens and yet, at the same time, seems almost tender, because the sagging breasts speak of a mother who has nursed many children.

Look at the necklace, which I promised you back at Tlatilco. It is made of open hands and human hearts, and from it hangs, at the center, a skull. The Mexica said that the Earth gave everything, but also claimed everything: the maize we eat comes from her, and when we die we return to her. That skull, which recalls the skulls of Teotihuacán and the lord of the dead, Mictlantecuhtli, is a reminder that every harvest has a price.

The skirt takes its name from its weave of rattlesnakes, and that is where her name comes from: coatl, serpent, and icue, skirt. Her arms end in serpent heads and her feet in eagle claws with feathers. She is a creature made from pieces of frightening animals, and yet she is conceived as a generous goddess. After the clay women of Tlatilco and the [Chalchiuhtlicue of Teotihuacán](mna_s04_chalchiuhtlicue), here is the most powerful of the family.

She has a secret beneath her feet. The underside of the sculpture, the part that touches the ground and that no one can see, is carved with another figure: that of [Tlaltecuhtli](mna_s06_tlaltecuhtli), the Earth, in a birthing posture. You will see one such piece in this hall in its entirety, and you will understand why the Mexica carved the Earth where she could feel it.

The modern history of Coatlicue is almost as dramatic as her myth. She was found on August 13, 1790, while workers were leveling the Main Square, in what is now the Zócalo. The viceregal authorities took her to the University, but her appearance made such an impression that they decided to bury her again, in one of the courtyards. It is said that people began to bring her flowers. Years later, the German scholar Alexander von Humboldt asked to see her, and she was unearthed for a while so that he could draw her.

The one who studied her most carefully was the New Spain astronomer Antonio de León y Gama, who described Coatlicue and the [Sun Stone](mna_s06_piedra_sol), found only a few months apart, as parts of one and the same universe. His book of 1792 is one of the first attempts to understand the Mexica world with a scientific spirit. In independent Mexico, Coatlicue was unearthed for good and passed to the National Museum.

That is why it is worth seeing her as a paradox: the most terrifying image in the museum is also that of a mother. And she is, at the same time, a symbol of survival. The Spaniards buried her, they did not destroy her, and that decision left us one of the great sculptures of the world.

texto: Count the two serpent heads that form the face
Find the skull hanging at the center of the necklace
Notice the eagle claws on her feet

texto.Dimensions: 2.52 m high x 1.30 m wide x 1.30 m deep

texto.pregunta: Myth: The Spaniards destroyed all the Mexica sculptures.
texto.respuesta: Reality: Many were buried instead of being broken, and that is why we can see them today. Coatlicue was buried twice before reaching the museum.
